q: Where is the Japanese bracketing system mainly used?
n: The Japanese bracketing system (tokyō) is used mainly in the roof system, to carry the deep projecting eaves. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Japanese architecture).

q: Which is true of Japanese column spacing?
n: Japanese column spacing follows the ken module (about 1.8 m), which also sets tatami and room sizes. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Global History of Architecture.

q: How do Chinese and Japanese pagodas typically differ in plan?
n: Chinese pagodas are commonly octagonal in plan, while Japanese pagodas are mostly square. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Chinese and Japanese pagodas).

q: What is the usual plan of a Chinese pagoda?
n: Chinese pagodas are typically octagonal in plan, especially the brick pagodas from the Song dynasty on. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What sets Japanese temples apart from Chinese ones?
n: Japanese temples favor natural, often unpainted timber and restrained ornament, while Chinese temples are richly painted and colored. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: The stupa comes from which architecture?
n: The stupa comes from Buddhist India, as a hemispherical mound enshrining relics. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Indian architecture).

q: What is traditionally seen as the origin of the pagoda?
n: The pagoda of East Asia is traditionally traced to the Indian stupa, transformed into a tower form. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Stupa building was chiefly developed by the:
n: Stupa building was developed chiefly by the Indians, notably under the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which is regarded as the oldest stupa, holding relics of the Buddha?
n: The Great Stupa at Sanchi, commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BC, is regarded as the oldest stone stupa and holds relics. Source: UNESCO (Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi).

q: What architectural feature often crowns the top of a stupa symbolizing enlightenment?
n: The chhatra (parasol) crowns the stupa above the harmika, symbolizing royalty and enlightenment. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Global History of Architecture.

q: Which temple complex is the largest religious monument in the world, first Hindu and later Buddhist?
n: Angkor Wat in Cambodia is the largest religious monument in the world. It was built as a Hindu temple for Suryavarman II and later became Buddhist. Source: UNESCO (Angkor); Guinness World Records.

q: Angkor Wat is the prime example of which architecture?
n: Angkor Wat is the prime example of Khmer architecture, at the height of the Khmer Empire. Source: UNESCO (Angkor); Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Masjid al-Haram is also called the:
o: Great Mosque of the Islamic World
n: Masjid al-Haram is the Great Mosque of Mecca, surrounding the Kaaba. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Great Mosque of Mecca.

q: Which part of a mosque is the screened enclosure near the mihrab?
n: The maqsura is a screened enclosure near the mihrab that protected the ruler during prayer. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Islamic architecture).

q: Which architecture produced stupas and rock-cut temples?
n: Indian architecture produced stupas and rock-cut temples and monasteries, as at Ajanta and Ellora. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; UNESCO (Ajanta, Ellora).

q: What type of structure is the Malwiya Minaret?
n: The Malwiya is a minaret, the tower from which the call to prayer is made, at the Great Mosque of Samarra. Source: UNESCO (Samarra Archaeological City).

q: What is the spiral minaret of the Great Mosque of Samarra called?
n: The spiral minaret of the Great Mosque of Samarra is the Malwiya Minaret ("snail shell"). Source: UNESCO (Samarra Archaeological City).

q: In which city is the Malwiya Minaret?
n: The Malwiya Minaret is in Samarra, Iraq, built in the 9th century under the Abbasids. Source: UNESCO (Samarra Archaeological City).

q: What is the main function of a minaret like the Malwiya?
n: A minaret such as the Malwiya is the tower from which the muezzin calls worshippers to prayer (the adhan). Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Minaret; UNESCO (Samarra).

q: Pagodas traditionally have how many stories?
n: Pagodas traditionally have an odd number of stories, usually 3, 5, 7, 9 or 13, following Buddhist numerology. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (pagodas).

q: What plan shape identifies most Japanese pagodas?
n: Most Japanese pagodas are square in plan and built of timber, such as the five-storey pagoda of Hōryū-ji. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; UNESCO (Hōryū-ji).

q: What is the main purpose of a pagoda?
n: A pagoda's main purpose is worship and enshrining sacred relics, inherited from the Indian stupa. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What distinguishes Chinese pagodas from Japanese pagodas in terms of structural design?
o: Japanese pagodas use steel instead of wood
Chinese pagodas are taller and more rigidly symmetrical
Chinese pagodas are shorter and simpler
Japanese pagodas are built entirely underground
n: Chinese pagodas, often of brick and octagonal, tend to be taller and more rigidly symmetrical. Japanese pagodas are timber, square and lower, with wide eaves. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is characteristic of Japanese architecture?
n: Japanese architecture is rectilinear and clean: post-and-beam timber frames, modular planning and restrained ornament. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Japanese architecture).

q: Best concert hall known for both exterior and interior design, as well as acoustics.
n: Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) is acclaimed for its stainless steel exterior, its warm wood interior and its acoustics by Yasuhisa Toyota. Source: LA Phil / Walt Disney Concert Hall official site.
